entries.title: Senate Spending Deal Pauses Trump’s Funding Power Grab. It Might Be Too Late.
entries.summary: The Trump administration has politicized federal grants without a formal rule.
entries.content:
In theory, the Trump administration suffered a major setback this week when senators moved to block the White House’s plans to exert more control over federal funds.

In practice, little has changed for an administration that has played politics with the federal grantmaking process from Day One.

This week, the Senate unveiled a bipartisan compromise to keep the government open through December. Democrats celebrated one major concession from the Republican majority as part of that deal: It would block the White House from finalizing a proposed rule to give political appointees firm control over every federal dollar and empower the White House to cancel grants for any reason at any time.

The temporary block won’t undo the Trump administration’s takeover of federal grants already underway.

Just last month, the Interior Department appointed Kristen Eastlick to serve as the agency's head of grants. She has spent much of her career seeking to expose nonprofit organizations as beholden to left-wing special interests.

She previously helped lead the Capital Research Center, frequently suggesting liberal groups masquerading as nonprofits too often receive federal dollars, and now she will help implement the Interior Department’s new political crackdown on grant funding that continues to tie up hundreds of millions of dollars in spending at National Parks and other departments.

Her new role, previously only held by career staffers, illustrates how the Trump administration continues to politicize grantmaking throughout government, even as it faces congressional pushback on its plans to codify those changes.

The White House’s proposed formal rule united the groups that have individually been battling the Trump administration’s attacks on their funding for the last 18 months. Nonprofits, cities, states, universities and the scientific research community called for Congress to act — and in a way, Congress responded.

But the problem for Congress is that blocking the rule does not stop the Trump administration from continuing to make the changes that the rule essentially formalized, current federal employees and former grant and budget officials told NOTUS.

"This is an unusual rule in so far as the most problematic things in it are all reflective of actions the administration has already been taking, and therefore reflective of authorities that the administration has already been claiming,” said Jacob Leibenluft, who served in the OMB at the end of the Biden administration. "This is as much codifying a set of approaches and actions that the administration is already taking as it is asserting new theories about how to approach grantmaking."

The pause on the rule is also temporary, lasting only as long as the spending bill itself, currently set to expire on Dec. 11.

OMB did not respond to a request for comment.

Mary Feeney, a professor at Arizona State University who led a large program at the National Science Foundation during the Biden administration, speculated that the short-term timing on the prohibition is convenient for Republicans who are up for reelection in November. Susan Collins, the Republican chair of the Appropriations Committee, is facing a tough fight for her seat in Maine and will be able to claim credit for the deal.

“I would expect that there are some actors in Congress who see this as beneficial to their individual campaign agenda. Like, I can use this as a talking point, or I can use this to show I did something,” Feeney said.

Even if Congress opts to extend the ban after the midterms are over, agencies are continuing to formally implement new layers of political review first introduced by DOGE.

Last year, the Education Department eliminated its grants policy and risk management offices as part of widespread layoffs. When it subsequently withheld $7 billion in grants on its usual July 1 release date — nearly 20% of the annual funding the department makes available to schools nationwide ahead of each school year — career staff left at Education were not consulted.

“We found out on the news,” said a former Education Department employee in a grants office. The same was true when later that year it barred up-front awards to five school districts in northern Virginia by placing them on “high-risk status” because they did not conform to administration’s views on gender identity.

The department, which is in the process of transferring much of its grants administration to other federal agencies as part of the effort to dismantle it, has cut out career staff from much of the grants process altogether. The Trump administration is also using the “suspensions and debarments” process to proactively prevent groups that don’t align with it from receiving grants, the former employee said, a departure from long-standing federal regulation that suggests agencies only ban entities after they have violated the law.

“From my experience being there, the politicals were all too happy to do it themselves,” the former employee said.

Interior last month introduced Eastlick to staff in an email by saying the new appointee would “lead DOI’s evolving grants administration.” The department recently reinforced its political review process, employees previously told NOTUS, with any award worth more than $50,000 requiring a sign-off from division leadership as well as two political appointees at the department. As of early June, more than 1,400 awards worth more than $360 million were caught up in the resulting backlog.

Two years prior, employees said, fewer than 10 grants sat in the queue.

One current National Park Service employee said that action from Congress does not change the fact that “grants and other financial assistance are continually under direct scrutiny by the department.”

The Health and Human Services Department also recently implemented new layers of political review, with funding opportunities requiring approval from Secretary Robert Kennnedy Jr.’s office and the White House before they go public. Internal documents, public records and employees all indicated the new spending regime was leading to unprecedented delays in releasing the funds.

Last month, HHS canceled without explanation more than $60 million in grants provided through its Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, a small office that funds research into how patients receive care.

Despite the actions already underway, lawmakers celebrated their agreement. Collins, who previously came out against the proposed rule, said she was pleased it prevented the measure from taking effect. Sen. Patty Murray (D-Washington), the top Democrat on the committee, led her colleagues in advocating for the provision.

“I pushed very hard and secured an important provision to prevent the Office of Management and Budget from implementing its corrupt new grants rule, which would require a Trump political appointee to sign off on every last federal grant and empower them to terminate any grant, at any point for any reason,” Murray said on the Senate floor on Monday before the stopgap spending bill easily cleared a procedural vote. “This disastrous rule would put politics above science when determining, for example, what cancer research grants to fund.”

Murray vowed to kill the rule outright as part of future spending negotiations.

Given how much the Trump administration continues to politicize the federal funding process, experts are divided on whether the prohibition is an achievement at all.

“Why would we think that one little piece of rulemaking or difference in congressional practice would have any effect? Because Congress hasn't been able to really do anything to stop the current agenda,” Feeney said.

Leibenluft, the former OMB official, said there could be value in the lawmakers’ efforts, even if it is largely symbolic. "The pushback, in an aggregate, is meaningful. It has the potential, at least, to create a framework when the administration does further specific actions, for the public and ultimately legislators to say: 'You know, this is exactly why we pushed back on the rule. You're not supposed to be doing this.'"

entries.title: Max Miller Says Mike Johnson Is 'Standing Behind Me'
entries.summary: The Ohio Republican told CNN’s Jake Tapper that all three women who accused him of violence are lying.
entries.content:
Rep. Max Miller said House Speaker Mike Johnson is standing behind him in his bid for reelection, in a Tuesday interview on CNN about allegations of abuse by several women, including his ex-wife.

“Speaker Mike Johnson, everyone else, they're standing behind me. No one has told me to get off the ballot, and that's because they know I can win this seat,” Miller (R-Ohio) told CNN’s Jake Tapper in the 23-minute conversation.

Johnson’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment about whether he supports Miller’s reelection campaign.

Miller said he has no plans to drop out of the race before the deadline despite facing growing calls to do so from within his party, including from his former father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). The House Ethics Committee has opened a probe into the allegations against Miller after the congressman requested an investigation on Tuesday, saying he thought it would “clear my name.”

Tapper pushed Miller on the mounting allegations from Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, who accused the Ohio congressman of domestic abuse and child abuse in court filings, as well as reports from an ex-girlfriend, former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham, and a 2021 Politico report about an alleged incident of violence against a female classmate during high school.

When asked if all three women independently lied, Miller said, “Yes, it's very easy.”

Miller said his side of the story has been taken out of context in other interviews. He also told Tapper his daughter once said, “I do not want to go to mommy’s” and “I do not feel safe” in audio he recorded.

Tapper said the network would not be able to air those recordings, and brought up a police report in which Emily Moreno said their child told her things like, “Daddy kill you,” and “Daddy’s house is scary.”

“I wish you could talk to my beautiful baby girl. She can't string together sentences like that. She's 2½ years old. She doesn't have the ability to articulate any of what you just said,” Miller responded, calling the claims an “entire fabrication of the truth.”

“You just told me that she had said she was scared to go to mommy’s house, but now you’re saying that she’s not capable of saying, ‘Daddy kill you,’” Tapper rebutted. “It seems like she’s either able to say one but not the other — that doesn’t make sense.”

Emily Moreno also accused Miller of using illegal drugs after finding needles in his bedroom. He told CNN they were for testosterone replacement therapy, and added that the last time he used illegal drugs was “several years ago.”

Miller said that like President Donald Trump — who was reelected despite facing “the most extreme allegations in the world” — he too could win his Ohio reelection campaign in November.

“For no second am I going to sit here and continue to be debased by false and baseless allegations and be pushed out of a seat I have worked so hard to represent and done a terrific job for our community,” Miller said.

Republicans are nonetheless walking a tightrope in this Ohio race. Miller is set to face Democrat Brian Poindexter, a former union ironworker, in November’s election. Poindexter was up by 5 percentage points, and 41% of voters had an unfavorable view of Miller, according to recent polling conducted by a Republican firm that was obtained and reviewed by NOTUS.

entries.title: Mike Lindell Steps Down From MyPillow to Focus on Minnesota Governor Campaign
entries.summary: The CEO is stepping away from his role to focus on his Republican primary after facing a new string of controversies this month.
entries.content:
MyPillow founder and CEO Mike Lindell says he’s stepping away from his post at the company to focus on the Minnesota governor’s race.

"After 22 years of leading MyPillow, I know the company is ready for its next chapter and I know Minnesota cannot wait," Lindell wrote in a press release. "This decision is not about walking away. It is about stepping forward to serve.”

Lindell rose to prominence for supporting President Donald Trump’s attempts to contest the results of the 2020 election and has faced a slate of lawsuits and legal challenges since — including during his current gubernatorial run. His decision to focus on the upcoming Aug. 11 primary comes as he battles questions about his residency eligibility and a campaign law violation lawsuit.

Lindell said the move will allow him to dedicate his “full time, energy, and attention" to the campaign and Minnesotans, while former MyPillow President James Furlong takes over as CEO — a position Lindell has held since he founded the company in 2004. He also reduced his stake in the company to a minority share, but he will remain on MyPillow's board of directors.

The Minnesota Republican Party last week asked state officials to clarify the residency rules concerning gubernatorial candidates after reports that Lindell was registered to vote in Texas — the second time in a month the state party has cast doubt upon his candidacy. According to Minnesota’s constitution, gubernatorial candidates must live in the state for at least one year before the election.

“The Republican Party does not want Minnesotans who vote for any candidate for Governor to find, after the fact, that their vote was effectively wasted because the candidate did not meet constitutional qualification that could and should have been clarified in advance,” Alex Plechash, the state party chair, wrote in a letter to the Minnesota secretary of state.

On Monday, Lindell sent TV station KSTP pay stubs that show he’s paid taxes in Minnesota since at least August 2025.

“I don’t know why Alex Plechash, or whatever his last name is, and what he has against me,” Lindell said. “But ever since I got Donald Trump, the president’s endorsement, he has viciously attacked.”

The Minnesota secretary of state’s office told the network it does not have the “investigative authority” to review residency claims and deferred to the state Supreme Court.

Lindell is currently facing a lawsuit alleging he violated campaign finance rules by distributing promotional pillows at a July 4th parade. He told WCCO the allegations were a “set-up hit job” and he felt “very confident that there was no violations."

Lindell's social media accounts have been banned or restricted by several platforms for pushing election fraud claims, including Twitter and YouTube in 2021. He launched multiple social media platforms in response to these restrictions. On Tuesday, Lindell said his Facebook advertising accounts had been restored after calling on Meta to look into his gubernatorial ads apparently being blocked by the platform.

Lindell, whom Trump endorsed in July, has also faced several legal actions related to his false claims that the 2020 election had been stolen, including a House committee subpoenaing his phone records in 2022 during its Jan. 6 probe.

Lindell targeted voting system companies with claims of election fraud, leading to a $1.3 billion lawsuit from Dominion Voting System, now known as Liberty Vote, in 2021. The voting hardware company confidentially settled its defamation suit earlier this month after a former Republican election official purchased the voting company in October.

In a separate case last year, a federal appeals court ruled Lindell did not have to pay a $5 million award to a software engineer after he mounted a “Prove Mike Wrong Challenge” over claims China interfered in the 2020 election.

A recent poll found Lindell leading the Republican field at 35%, followed by Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth at 26% and Kendall Qualls, who earned the state party's endorsement, at 11%.

Whichever candidate wins the GOP nomination is likely to face Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who has steadily outraised her Republican opponents.

entries.title: Todd Blanche's Nomination Is in Jeopardy After Sen. Collins Says She'll Vote No
entries.summary: The acting attorney general needs to secure one more vote from either of two Republican holdouts: Cassidy or Murkowski.
entries.content:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche has moved to within a single vote of winning confirmation to lead the Justice Department, but his path narrowed after Maine Sen. Susan Collins, one of three remaining Republican holdouts, announced Tuesday evening she will vote against his nomination as it finally heads toward the Senate floor.

“While I believe Mr. Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political. Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the Department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation,” Collins said in a statement.

After weeks of intense talks, the acting attorney general finally cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday morning, having struck a deal over the weekend with Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) to nix a controversial “anti-weaponization fund” and limit the scope of President Donald Trump’s audit immunity deal with the IRS.

However, he got a mixed bag of results after that committee vote. Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) handed him a boost by announcing he would support Blanche on the floor. Hours later, though, Collins revealed that she will oppose him.

This puts Blanche on a tightrope, as he must win over at least one of the two remaining holdouts to be confirmed.

Collins nodded at Blanche’s initial decision to green-light a settlement with Trump that created the $1.8 billion Justice Department fund, which drew significant derision among Senate Republicans, and the immunity deal that would have shielded Trump from future IRS audit scrutiny, as key reasons for her decision.

However, she went even further, pointing to Blanche’s reported plan to roll back abortion access and the DOJ’s attempt to indict Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) over “their ill-advised, but constitutionally protected, videos” encouraging military members to resist unlawful orders.

“For these reasons, I will vote against this nomination,” she said.

Before Curtis gave his support Tuesday, he had indicated that his decision hinged on the deal secured by Cornyn and Tillis. He met with Blanche last week.

“I’ve been pleased with his receptivity and understanding of the issues raised by my colleagues and me, including the anti-weaponization fund and a number of Utah-specific priorities,” he said in a social media post. “I look forward to working with him once confirmed.”

With Collins and Curtis going public, that leaves two outstanding Senate Republicans who are undecided: Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy.

Murkowski, a preeminent centrist vote, told reporters that she is “going to have to have a few more conversations” with Blanche, but called the order killing the “anti-weaponization” fund a “pretty good step” on Monday.

“I’m going to find out more. I’d like to find out a little bit more about the negotiations over the weekend and I haven’t had a chance to do that,” she said, conceding that it “says a lot” that the pair of Judiciary Committee members made the deal.

Cassidy declined to comment repeatedly when pressed about Blanche.

Blanche and Republicans can lose no more than two votes on the floor due to Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Kentucky) ongoing absence, assuming there is full attendance otherwise.

The timing of a floor vote is also unclear. Senate GOP leaders have an ambitious agenda to complete before the chamber breaks for the five-week recess.

Senate leaders are trying to get unanimous consent to expedite passage of a stopgap spending bill through mid-December and the Russia sanctions package that won massive bipartisan support in an initial vote last week. They are also attempting to get the ball rolling on a cryptocurrency regulation bill and legislation protecting college athletes before departing town.

However, Blanche appears to be a priority. One Senate GOP aide, who requested anonymity to discuss private leadership plans, said there is a high likelihood that Blanche’s confirmation gets completed — which could keep the chamber in session into the weekend.

Tuesday’s committee vote took place only days after Chair Chuck Grassley was forced to cancel a vote late last week. Cornyn and Tillis finally struck a deal with Blanche and the Justice Department late Sunday, with both members emphasizing that it was not simply made for their benefit, as others in the Senate Republican conference have been worried about the proposed fund.

“Their concerns about the anti-weaponization fund and the IRS settlement were shared by many, including this senator,” Grassley said during Tuesday’s markup. “I am grateful that they, as well as Mr. Blanche and the White House, worked in good faith to resolve them. Formally rescinding the anti-weaponization fund and clarifying the scope of the release of claims has put this issue to bed once and for all."

Beyond Curtis, Blanche has picked up other key votes in recent days. Sens. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), a pair of incumbents who are up for reelection in November, both signaled that they plan to support him.

Husted told Punchbowl News that he is a “yes” vote pending a read-through of the deal struck with Cornyn and Tillis.

Sullivan noted that Blanche traveled to Alaska in recent weeks in an effort to “understand our state, understand the challenges either before or after your confirmation, and he did that.”

“He’s committed to working on a bunch of issues that really matter to Alaska,” Sullivan told NOTUS. “So I’m supportive.”

entries.title: Maryland Lawmakers Open the Door for 2028 Redistricting
entries.summary: The constitutional amendment would make it harder for any future redistricting efforts to be challenged in court, which had worried some Democrats.
entries.content:
Maryland lawmakers took a first step toward redrawing their congressional map during a special session on Tuesday, passing a constitutional amendment that could open the door for Democrats to pick up the only Republican seat in the state’s nine-member congressional delegation ahead of 2028.

Democrats in the Maryland General Assembly pushed through a constitutional amendment in both chambers that is aimed at shielding a possible redistricting effort from potential litigation. If approved by voters in November, the constitutional amendment would set a different standard for how the state draws its congressional districts compared with its assembly districts.

“We have seen how the federal government has told Republican states that they should do mid-decade redistricting but told Democratic states to sit on our hands,” Democratic Gov. Wes Moore said at a Monday press conference ahead of the legislative special session. “We have seen how the Voting Rights Act has fallen, which we predicted would happen at the start of this year. So we are back now to be able to ensure that our elections should be in the hands of the people of Maryland. They should have the final say.”

When Democrats attempted to redraw Maryland’s lines in 2022, a Maryland state court struck down the maps, calling the proposed maps a “product of extreme partisan gerrymandering.” State Senate President Bill Ferguson has repeatedly cited the 2022 decision as evidence that any redistricting effort would not withstand a legal challenge. The new bill aims to clarify that the requirements set by the 2022 ruling only apply to General Assembly seats, making it easier to pass a congressional gerrymander.

“This decision put Maryland in a very different position than many other states in this union and unless we address this uncertainty first, any other action would jeopardize our state’s current map,” Ferguson said of the 2022 ruling at a press conference on Monday before the session began.

Ferguson, who had been vocally opposed to redistricting in his state for months, pointed to the Supreme Court’s Louisiana v. Callais ruling as the ultimate driving force that led him to call for legislative action.

“A legal earthquake changed the landscape this spring when the Supreme Court of the United States, under Callais, eviscerated the very purpose and function of our Voting Rights Act,” Ferguson continued. “Even worse, we saw states like Tennessee, Louisiana and South Carolina act with haste to attempt to eliminate majority-minority congressional districts. These acts changed the calculus and that’s why we’re here.”

Maryland is the latest Democrat-led state to consider redistricting ahead of 2028 after a whirlwind year of redistricting that began last summer when President Donald Trump called on GOP lawmakers to redraw their maps to favor Republicans ahead of this year’s midterms and intensified following the Supreme Court’s April decision.

The only Democratic state that successfully redistricted was California, netting up to five seats after voters approved a ballot measure on the issue last November. The New York State Assembly advanced a constitutional amendment in June that opened up the possibility for Democrats to gain up to four House seats in 2028.

Conversations have swirled around redistricting in Maryland for months, with many Democrats urging the state to redraw their lines to oust the lone Republican representative in the seat, Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of the House Freedom Caucus who currently represents the Eastern Shore. In November, Moore created a Redistricting Advisory Commission, chaired by U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland), which ultimately recommended a redrawn map in January. The state House of Delegates approved the map, but Ferguson never brought the measure to the state Senate floor during the regular session.

NOTUS reported that Ferguson had begun talking with allies about how to move forward with redistricting after the Supreme Court decision, ultimately calling this summer’s special legislative session with House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk to consider the redistricting amendment.
